paper: Yamaguchi H, Suzuki S, Osana Y, Kawachi M. Complete Genome Sequence of Microcystis aeruginosa NIES-2481 and Common Genomic Features of Group G M. aeruginosa. Journal of Genomics 6:30-33 (2018). DOI 10.7150/jgen.24935.
organism: Microcystis aeruginosa NIES-2481 (freshwater bloom-forming cyanobacterium, group G, isolated from Lake Kasumigaura, Japan)

open_questions.q: Do the 28 antiSMASH secondary-metabolite biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) predictions in NIES-2481 (paper claim, not re-run in this replication) hold up against a current antiSMASH v7+ analysis, and if so are aeruginosin, micropeptin, and microviridin encoded by the same NRPS/PKS module architectures as in the well-studied M. aeruginosa NIES-843 and PCC 7806 genomes?
open_questions.basis: The paper asserts 28 antiSMASH clusters and specifically calls out aeruginosin, micropeptin, and microviridin as present, but this replication only confirmed rich NRPS content indirectly via 117 low-identity mcyA cross-hits (best ~42% pid). Neither the paper nor this replication reports current antiSMASH BGC boundaries, module counts, or ortholog assignments for NIES-2481.
open_questions.next_steps: Run antiSMASH v7+ on CP012375 + CP025929 on uicgpu (GPU not required; a spare A100 slot is fine); tabulate cluster count, cluster class, and top MIBiG hit per cluster; do pairwise NRPS-module BLAST against NIES-843 aeruginosin/micropeptin/microviridin references to assess conservation of module order and A-domain specificity.

open_questions.q: How many CRISPR-Cas loci and of which subtype (I-D vs III-B are common in Microcystis) are actually present in NIES-2481, are their spacer sets shared with sister strain NIES-2549, and do any spacers match known cyanophages (Ma-LMM01, MaMV-DC, or the S-CBP series) that predate on Microcystis?
open_questions.basis: The paper claims 5 CRISPR loci but gives no subtype breakdown, no spacer counts, and no phage-target analysis. This replication left C15 out of scope. Microcystis-cyanophage co-evolution is a live topic in freshwater microbial ecology, and shared spacers between NIES-2481 and NIES-2549 would be direct evidence for their shared ecological history in Lake Kasumigaura.
open_questions.next_steps: Run CRISPRCasFinder (or the newer CRISPRCasTyper) on CP012375 for both strains; extract spacer FASTAs; blastn each spacer set against the NCBI cyanophage genome collection (Ma-LMM01 NC_008562, MaMV-DC, plus any complete Microcystis-infecting phage in GenBank as of 2026); compute Jaccard similarity of spacer sets between NIES-2481 and NIES-2549.

open_questions.q: Given that NIES-2481 and NIES-2549 have 100.0% identical 16S rRNA and are both group-G, non-toxic (mcy-negative) Lake Kasumigaura isolates, what is their whole-genome ANI (average nucleotide identity), and does the ANI cross the 95-96% species-demarcation threshold cleanly or reveal them as effectively clonal isolates of the same strain lineage?
open_questions.basis: 16S identity of 100% is common among Microcystis strains (16S is famously poor at resolving Microcystis at the strain/species level; this is a known limitation of the genus) and does not by itself establish clonality. Chromosome-size difference is only 1,207 bp (0.03%), which is suspiciously small and hints at extremely close ancestry, but the report never computes ANI or dDDH.
open_questions.next_steps: Compute ANI between CP012375 (NIES-2481) and CP011304 (NIES-2549) with fastANI and pyani (ANIb+ANIm); compute in-silico dDDH via TYGS; separately compare their plasmids (147,539 bp vs 6,987 bp) — the ~20x plasmid-size disparity in otherwise near-identical genomes is a striking asymmetry worth explaining (plasmid gain in NIES-2481? loss in NIES-2549?).

open_questions.q: Is the mobilome (transposases, insertion sequences, and integrative-conjugative elements) that the report notes as enriched in NIES-2481 (34 transposase-labeled CDS) responsible for the ~1.2 kb chromosome-size delta and, more interestingly, for the plasmid-size delta between NIES-2481 (147,539 bp) and NIES-2549 (6,987 bp)?
open_questions.basis: The report spot-checked transposase-CDS count (34) as consistent with the paper's Table 2 enrichment claim, but no IS-element-level or ICE-level analysis was done. Cyanobacterial group-G strains are known to carry variable IS-element loads, and a 140+ kb plasmid-size difference between otherwise near-clonal strains would typically require large mobile-element insertions or plasmid fusion/deletion events.
open_questions.next_steps: Run ISEScan or digIS on both CP012375 and CP011304 to enumerate and classify IS families; run ICEfinder for integrative-conjugative elements; align the two plasmids (CP025929 vs CP026286) with nucmer/MUMmer to identify which regions are unique to the 147 kb NIES-2481 plasmid; check whether the unique regions have IS/transposase flanking signatures consistent with recent acquisition.

open_questions.q: M. aeruginosa is famous for producing microcystin, yet NIES-2481 (and its sister NIES-2549) is confirmed mcy-negative — is this because they carry a degenerate/pseudogenized mcy cluster remnant (loss-of-function) or because the mcy cluster was never present in the group-G lineage (never-acquired), and can this be resolved by looking for syntenic mcy-flanking genes without the mcy ORFs themselves?
open_questions.basis: This replication's strict-orthology tblastn returned 0 hits, which cleanly confirms the paper's absence claim but does not distinguish 'loss' from 'never had it.' In M. aeruginosa strain PCC 7005 (and others), a partial mcy remnant with flanking uma1/uma2/... genes has been reported as evidence of secondary loss; the group-G Lake Kasumigaura non-toxic phenotype's evolutionary origin is genuinely open in the Microcystis literature.
open_questions.next_steps: Extract the mcy cluster flanking regions (uma1/uma2/dnaN-region) from a canonical mcy+ reference (NIES-843 or PCC 7806) and blastn them against CP012375; check for syntenic conservation with no intervening mcy ORFs (= loss) vs no flanking synteny at all (= never had it); reciprocal-best-hit analysis of all mcy operon genes (mcyA-J) at relaxed identity (>=30%) to detect pseudogene fragments; place NIES-2481 on a group-G phylogeny of mcy presence/absence to estimate the ancestral state.
